{{Short description|Geometric shape}}
{{for|the music album|Semicircle (album)}}
{{Infobox polygon|image=Semicircle-curve.svg|name=Semicircle|area={{sfrac|πr<sup>2</sup>|2}}|perimeter={{math|(π+2)r}}}}

In [[mathematics]] (and more specifically [[geometry]]), a '''semicircle''' is a one-dimensional [[Locus (mathematics)|locus]] of points that forms half of a [[circle]]. It is a [[circular arc]] that measures 180° (equivalently, {{pi}} [[radians]], or a [[turn (geometry)#Subdivision of turns|half-turn]]). It only has one line of symmetry ([[reflection symmetry]]).

In non-technical usage, the term "semicircle" is sometimes used to refer to either a [[closed curve]] that also includes the diameter segment from one end of the arc to the other or to the half-[[Disc (geometry)|disk]], which is a two-dimensional [[Region (mathematics)|geometric region]] that further includes all the interior points.

By [[Thales' theorem]], any [[triangle]] [[Inscribed figure|inscribed]] in a semicircle with a [[vertex (geometry)|vertex]] at each of the endpoints of the semicircle and the third vertex elsewhere on the semicircle is a [[right triangle]], with a [[right angle]] at the third vertex.

All lines intersecting the semicircle [[perpendicular]]ly are [[concurrent lines|concurrent]] at the center of the circle containing the given semicircle.

==Arithmetic and geometric means==
[[File:quadrature_of_rectangle.svg|thumb|left|upright|Construction of a square with the same area as a given oblong]]
{{AM_GM_inequality_visual_proof.svg}}
A semicircle can be used to [[Compass and straightedge constructions|construct]] the [[arithmetic mean|arithmetic]] and [[geometric mean|geometric]] means of two lengths using straight-edge and compass. For a semicircle with a diameter of ''a'' + ''b'', the length of its [[radius]] is the arithmetic mean of ''a'' and ''b'' (since the radius is half of the diameter).

The [[geometric mean]] can be found by dividing the diameter into two segments of lengths ''a'' and ''b'', and then connecting their common endpoint to the semicircle with a segment perpendicular to the diameter. The length of the resulting segment is the geometric mean. This can be proven by applying the [[Pythagorean theorem]] to three similar right triangles, each having as vertices the point where the perpendicular touches the semicircle and two of the three endpoints of the segments of lengths ''a'' and ''b''.<ref>[http://aleph0.clarku.edu/~djoyce/java/elements/bookVI/propVI13.html Euclid's Elements, Book VI, Proposition 13]</ref>

The construction of the geometric mean can be used to transform any rectangle into a square of the same area, a problem called the [[Quadrature (geometry)|quadrature]] of a rectangle. The side length of the square is the geometric mean of the side lengths of the rectangle. More generally, it is used as a [[Lemma (mathematics)|lemma]] in a general method for transforming any polygonal shape into a similar copy of itself with the area of any other given polygonal shape.<ref>[https://mathcs.clarku.edu/~djoyce/java/elements/bookVI/propVI25.html Euclid's Elements, Book VI, Proposition 25]</ref>{{clear|left}}

==Farey diagram==
[[File:Comparison_Ford_circles_Farey_diagram.svg|thumb|upright=1.35|link={{filepath:comparison_Ford_circles_Farey_diagram.svg}}|Comparison of Ford circles and a Farey diagram with semicircles for ''n'' from 1 to 9. Each semicircle intersects its corresponding circles at right angles. {{nowrap|In [{{filepath:comparison_Ford_circles_Farey_diagram.svg}} the SVG image,]}} hover over a circle or curve to highlight it and its terms.]]
The [[Farey sequence]] of order ''n'' is the [[sequence]] of completely reduced [[fraction]]s which when [[in lowest terms]] have [[denominator]]s less than or equal to ''n'', arranged in order of increasing size. With a restricted definition, each Farey sequence starts with the value 0, denoted by the fraction {{sfrac|0|1}}, and ends with the fraction {{sfrac|1}}. [[Ford circle]]s can be constructed [[tangent]] to their neighbours, and to the x-axis at these points. Semicircles joining adjacent points on the x-axis pass through the points of contact at right angles.<ref>{{cite web | url=http://mathworld.wolfram.com/FordCircle.html | title=Ford Circle }}</ref>

==Equation==

The equation of a semicircle with radius <math>r</math> and midpoint <math>(x_0, y_0)</math> on the diameter between its endpoints and which is entirely concave from below is
<math display="block">
 y = y_0 + \sqrt{r^2 - (x - x_0)^2}.
</math>

If it is entirely concave from above, the equation is
<math display="block">
 y = y_0 - \sqrt{r^2 - (x - x_0)^2}.
</math>

==Arbelos==
[[Image:Arbelos.svg|thumb|An '''arbelos''' (grey region)]]
An [[arbelos]] is a region in the [[plane (geometry)|plane]] bounded by three semicircles connected at their endpoints, all on the same side of a [[straight line]] (the ''baseline'') that contains their [[diameter]]s.
